## QUESTION 1

__Write an SQL query that provides playerID, yearID, and batting average for players with at least 1 at bat that year. Sort the table from highest batting average to lowest, and then by playerid alphabetically. Show the top 5 results in your report.__

The data that the returned table reflects shows 5 names all that start with a and that have a batting average of 1.0. Because of the filter letting data in as long as a player has just 1 at bat, means the data the table is displaying is most likely those that went to bat once that year, hit the ball when they were at bat and then didn't bat again for the rest of the year. This would explain the perfect batting average for every player, and why they're all a names as the table is sorted alphabetically.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here

# The code below can serve as a template for all the rest of your queries. It is just missing the
# SQL code. Put your SQL query in between the triple quotation marks to create the query. The records will be stored in 'results', which is a polars data frame

q = """
    SELECT playerID, yearID, SUM(H) * 1.0 / SUM(AB) AS `Batting Average`
    FROM batting
    GROUP BY playerID, yearID 
    HAVING SUM(AB) >= 1
    ORDER BY `Batting Average` DESC, playerID
    LIMIT 5;
    """
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results


```


## QUESTION 2

__Use the same query as above, but only include players with at least 10 at bats that year. Print the top 5 results.__  

The table this time is much more what I would expect. The batting Average for all 5 sits within a range of 0.56 - 0.64. The best Average being the player nymanny01 with an Average of 0.642857.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here

q = """
    SELECT playerID, yearID, SUM(H) * 1.0 / SUM(AB) AS `Batting Average`
    FROM batting
    GROUP BY playerID, yearID 
    HAVING SUM(AB) >= 10
    ORDER BY `Batting Average` DESC, playerID
    LIMIT 5;
    """
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results
```


## QUESTION 3

__Now modify the SQL query to calculate the batting average for players over their entire careers (all years combined). Only include players with at least 100 at bats over their entire career, and print the top 5 results.__

When filtered down to lifetime results Batting Averages dropped by about half to a range of 0.356-0.366 for the top 5. The best being the player cobbty01 with an Average of 0.3663.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here

q = """
    SELECT playerID, SUM(H) * 1.0 / SUM(AB) AS `Batting Average`
    FROM batting
    GROUP BY playerID 
    HAVING SUM(AB) >= 100
    ORDER BY `Batting Average` DESC, playerID
    LIMIT 5;
    """
results = pl.read_database(q, con)
results
```
